name: Ria Health
one_liner: Online alcohol treatment with a doctor, medication such as naltrexone, coaching and a connected breathalyzer, to cut back or quit.
best_for: Adults who want medication and coaching to drink less, not only to quit
People whose insurance has Ria in network
People who want to track progress with a connected breathalyzer
not_for: Anyone in crisis: call or text 988, or call 911
People who may have dangerous alcohol withdrawal and need medical detox
People who need treatment for drugs other than alcohol
short_description: Telehealth alcohol treatment combining prescribed medication, coaching and breathalyzer tracking; in-network with some insurers.
long_description: Ria Health is a US telehealth program for alcohol use disorder. Members see a medical provider by video who can prescribe anti-craving medication such as naltrexone, meet with a recovery coach, and log blood alcohol readings with a Bluetooth breathalyzer in its app; the goal can be moderation or abstinence. It is reported to be available in all 50 states and is in-network with some insurers (including Anthem/BCBS, UnitedHealthcare/Optum, Oxford and Carelon), but not Medicaid. Ria does not publish self-pay prices; reviews report about $175 to $449 a month, and reviewers often mention billing and cancellation complaints. Two uncontrolled studies of Ria members, co-authored by company staff, reported lower breathalyzer readings among people who stayed in the program for 90 days, with about half still enrolled at 90 days in the first study; there is no randomized trial.

pricing.starting_price: Copay with insurance; self-pay reported at about $175–$449/month (not published by Ria)
pricing.notes: Ria says cost depends on your insurance and the plan you choose; the self-pay range is from third-party reviews. Medication pharmacy costs may be separate (Ria estimates $25–$60/month for oral naltrexone).

privacy.notes: Policy (Aug 2025) says it does not sell personal information under the CCPA but uses advertising and targeting cookies on riahealth.com (not member sites); member health information falls under its HIPAA notice.

faqs.a: No, Ria Health meets you where you are. Some people want to quit alcohol completely; others want to reduce to moderate drinking. The program supports both goals using evidence-based medication and coaching. You define what success looks like for you.

faqs.q: What medications does Ria Health use?
faqs.a: Ria primarily uses naltrexone, which reduces cravings and the reward from drinking. Other FDA-approved medications may be used depending on your situation. The Sinclair Method (naltrexone before drinking) is one approach they support.
Yes, Ria accepts many major insurance plans. Coverage varies by plan and state. They also offer self-pay options. Contact them to verify your specific insurance benefits before enrolling.

faqs.q: How is Ria different from AA?
faqs.a: AA is a peer support program emphasizing abstinence and spirituality. Ria is medical treatment using FDA-approved medications with professional coaching. They can complement each other—some people use both. Ria doesn't require abstinence or spiritual components.

patient_summary: You meet a Ria doctor by video, who may prescribe medication such as naltrexone, and you have regular coaching sessions and check your blood alcohol with a connected breathalyzer in the Ria app. Your goal can be drinking less or stopping. Cost depends on your insurance; Ria does not publish self-pay prices.
